claims.text: Increasing the copper fraction relative to chromium reduces local cohesive energy in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Increasing the copper fraction relative to chromium promotes short-range atomic disorder.
Reduced cohesive energy and increased short-range disorder lower the onset temperatures of premelting and melting.
Equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles can initially form a homogeneously mixed, single-phase solid solution.
Changing the chromium-to-copper balance produces changes in local atomic ordering, chemical clustering, and defect density.
Copper has a lower melting point than chromium.
Copper has higher atomic mobility than the more refractory constituents represented by chromium.
Increasing copper disrupts the uniform lattice of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu solid solution.
Copper-induced local disorder accelerates atomic diffusion at lower temperatures.
Faster low-temperature diffusion facilitates an earlier onset of premelting.
Changing elemental composition can shift thermodynamic energy contributions and melting enthalpy relative to a baseline material.
Copper-enriched Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a statistically significant reduction in premelting onset temperature relative to equimolar particles.
Copper enrichment will produce a corresponding shift in melting enthalpy.
Chromium-rich Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a higher premelting onset temperature than the equimolar baseline.
An inert or vacuum atmosphere prevents oxidation during the thermal ramp.
Rapid heat–cool cycles minimize extrinsic effects such as oxidation or sintering.
Nanoparticle size distribution and heating rate may influence the observed premelting and melting trends.
